title: Voyager
blurb: Launched in 1977, the twin Voyager probes are the most distant human-made objects ever — now drifting through interstellar space, more than 24 billion km from home, still faintly calling back to Earth.

title: The Sun
sub: A furnace fusing 600M tonnes a second
blurb: Our star is a ball of glowing plasma 1.39 million km across, holding 99.86% of all the mass in the solar system. Every second it fuses some 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium — the light and warmth of every world.

title: The Space Station
blurb: The International Space Station is the largest structure humans have ever put in space — about the size of a football field. It races around Earth at 27,600 km/h, so its crew sees a sunrise or sunset every 45 minutes.

title: Starships to Come
sub: The engines that might reach a star
blurb: No craft yet built could cross to another star in a lifetime. Concepts — fusion rockets, ion drives, and vast light-sails pushed by lasers — imagine vehicles that could one day travel a tenth of the speed of light.

title: Olympus Mons
blurb: Olympus Mons on Mars is the tallest known volcano in the solar system: about 22 km high, two and a half times the height of Everest, on a base roughly the size of Arizona. Low gravity and a still crust let it grow for millions of years.

title: Black Holes
blurb: A black hole crams so much mass into so little space that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the event horizon. The supermassive one at the heart of our galaxy, Sagittarius A*, weighs about 4 million Suns.

title: Wormholes
blurb: A wormhole — an Einstein-Rosen bridge — is a hypothetical tunnel joining two distant points in spacetime, a shortcut permitted by Einstein's equations. None has ever been observed, and holding one open would demand strange "exotic" matter.

title: Pulsars
sub: A city-sized star spinning hundreds of times a second
blurb: When a giant star dies it can leave behind a neutron star — the densest object in the universe, an entire Sun crushed into a ball the size of a city. Some spin hundreds of times a second, sweeping beams of radio light past Earth like a cosmic lighthouse.

title: Neutron Stars
sub: A whole Sun crushed into a city
blurb: When a giant star's core collapses it can crush the mass of an entire Sun into a sphere just 20 km across — the densest matter in the universe short of a black hole. A single teaspoon of it would weigh about a billion tonnes, and its surface gravity is billions of times Earth's.

title: Supernova
sub: A dying star outshines a whole galaxy
blurb: When a massive star runs out of fuel its core collapses and it detonates as a supernova — for a few weeks blazing brighter than its entire galaxy, and forging the heavy elements that go on to build planets and people.

title: The Milky Way
sub: Our home — a hundred billion suns
blurb: The Milky Way is our home galaxy: a vast spiral roughly 100,000 light-years across, holding a few hundred billion stars. Our Sun is just one of them, riding a quiet outer arm and taking about 225 million years to circle the galactic centre once.

title: Comets
sub: Icy wanderers that grow tails near the Sun
blurb: A comet is a chunk of ice and dust left over from the birth of the solar system. As it swings near the Sun it heats up and streams two glowing tails — always pointing away from the Sun — that can stretch tens of millions of kilometres.

title: Total Eclipse
sub: The Moon perfectly hides the Sun
blurb: By sheer cosmic coincidence the Moon and Sun look almost exactly the same size in our sky. When the Moon slips perfectly in front, day fades to dusk and the Sun's ghostly corona blazes into view for a few breathtaking minutes.

title: The Kuiper Belt
blurb: Past Neptune lies the Kuiper Belt — a vast doughnut of icy worlds left over from the dawn of the solar system. Pluto is its most famous resident, but it holds thousands of frozen bodies and likely far more still uncharted.

title: Saturn's Hexagon
sub: A six-sided storm at the north pole
blurb: Crowning Saturn's north pole is a bizarre six-sided jet stream wider than two Earths — a stable hexagon of racing cloud that has held its shape for as long as we have watched, with a swirling cyclone at its heart.

title: Rogue Planets
sub: Starless worlds adrift in the dark
blurb: Not every planet circles a star. Cast out of their birth systems, rogue planets drift alone through interstellar space in perpetual night — and there may be billions of them wandering the galaxy, more than the stars themselves.
